cls: Urologic (genitourinary) irrigating solution - non-electrolyte amino-acid irrigant
pharm: A sterile, non-conductive, approximately isosmotic 1.5% solution of the amino acid glycine used to irrigate and distend the surgical field; being free of electrolytes it does not conduct the electrosurgical current used in transurethral resection.
quick: 1.5% solution used in volumes needed to irrigate/distend the surgical field; not for IV infusion
Use only if clearly needed; limited data
Caution - reduced clearance increases fluid-overload/hyponatremia risk
Caution - impaired glycine/ammonia metabolism may worsen toxicity
Fluid balance, serum sodium/electrolytes, signs of TUR syndrome, ammonia
summary: Glycine 1.5% Irrigation is a sterile, non-pyrogenic, electrolyte-free (non-conductive) urologic irrigating solution used to irrigate and maintain visibility of the surgical field during transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) and other transurethral electrosurgical procedures. Because it contains no electrolytes, it does not disperse the high-frequency cutting current. It is for irrigation only and must NOT be given intravenously. Its principal hazard is systemic absorption of large volumes through opened venous sinuses, producing dilutional hyponatremia and fluid overload (the transurethral resection or TUR syndrome), with hypervolemia, hyponatremia, visual disturbances, confusion, and from glycine/ammonia metabolism possible encephalopathy. Risk rises with prolonged resection, high irrigation pressure/height, and large absorbed volumes, so fluid balance, serum sodium and signs of TUR syndrome must be monitored closely.
indications: Urologic irrigation to maintain visibility and distend the operative field during transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) and other transurethral surgical (electrosurgical) procedures

dosage.d: Volume of 1.5% glycine solution as required to irrigate and distend the operative field during the procedure
dosage.n: NOT for intravenous injection; minimise volume and pressure absorbed

dosage.d: As clinically required for continued irrigation
dosage.n: Monitor for absorption and fluid overload

admin: Use only if the solution is clear and the container undamaged; intended for urologic irrigation only - do NOT administer intravenously
Warm to near body temperature where appropriate, and use aseptic technique; discard unused portion (single-use)
Limit the height of the irrigation reservoir (irrigation pressure) and the duration of resection to minimise systemic absorption through opened venous sinuses
Monitor the volume instilled versus recovered and the patient's fluid balance during and after the procedure
Watch for signs of the transurethral resection (TUR) syndrome - hypertension then hypotension, bradycardia, nausea, confusion, visual disturbance
Check serum sodium and electrolytes if absorption is suspected or the procedure is prolonged
moa: Glycine 1.5% is a non-electrolyte (non-ionic), nearly isosmotic solution whose function during transurethral electrosurgery is physical and electrical rather than pharmacologic: it distends and continuously washes the operative field to maintain endoscopic visibility, and because it lacks electrolytes it does not conduct the high-frequency current used for cutting and coagulation, allowing effective electrosurgery. When large volumes are absorbed into the circulation through open prostatic venous sinuses, the glycine and free water are distributed and metabolized; the resulting dilution of serum sodium and the metabolic products of glycine (including ammonia and glyoxylate) account for the systemic features of TUR syndrome.

absolute: Intravenous administration (solution is for irrigation only)
relative: Significant renal impairment (reduced ability to clear absorbed fluid)
Conditions predisposing to large irrigant absorption (long resection, large prostate, open sinuses)
monitor: Cardiovascular and neurologic status (signs of TUR syndrome)
Serum ammonia if encephalopathy is suspected

preg: There are no adequate data on the use of glycine irrigating solution in pregnancy; systemic effects would only arise from absorption during a procedure. Use only if clearly needed and with careful attention to fluid and electrolyte balance.
lact: There are limited data; significant systemic exposure occurs only with absorption during irrigation. Use with caution in breastfeeding women.
renal: Patients with impaired renal function have a reduced ability to excrete absorbed free water and glycine, increasing the risk of fluid overload and dilutional hyponatremia. Use with particular caution and monitor fluid balance and serum sodium closely.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment may reduce metabolism of absorbed glycine and clearance of ammonia, potentially worsening encephalopathic features of TUR syndrome; use with caution and monitor neurologic status and ammonia.

moderate: No characteristic drug-drug interactions; systemic effects derive from volume/electrolyte changes rather than pharmacologic interaction
minor: Diuretics may be used to manage fluid overload from absorbed irrigant
interactions.diagnostics: Significant absorption lowers serum sodium and serum osmolality (dilutional hyponatremia) and may raise serum ammonia and glycine.

common: Transient irrigant absorption (usually subclinical with small volumes)
serious: Transurethral resection (TUR) syndrome - dilutional hyponatremia, hypervolemia/fluid overload, hypertension then hypotension, bradycardia
Pulmonary edema and congestive heart failure from fluid overload
Cerebral edema with confusion, seizures and coma
Transient visual disturbance/blindness (glycine effect on the retina)
emergency: Acute TUR syndrome (severe hyponatremia with neurologic deterioration, seizures)

monitoring: Intraoperative and postoperative fluid balance (irrigant instilled versus recovered)
Serum sodium and electrolytes, especially with prolonged or extensive resection
Cardiovascular signs (blood pressure, heart rate) and respiratory status
counsel: This fluid is used during your prostate or bladder surgery to keep the surgical area clear - it is not a medicine you take by mouth
After the procedure tell the staff if you feel confused, sick, develop blurred vision or a bad headache, or have trouble breathing
You may have continuous bladder washing for a time after surgery; let the nurses know about any swelling or breathlessness
The team will check your blood salts and fluid balance after the operation
pk: Acts immediately as a surgical irrigant; systemic effects appear only if absorbed (often during/soon after resection)
Plasma sodium/osmolality changes peak around the time of greatest absorption
Absorbed glycine is metabolized over hours; free water cleared by the kidneys
TUR-syndrome effects persist until fluid/electrolyte balance is corrected
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from freezing; single-use, discard unused portion
pearls: Glycine 1.5% irrigation IS an FDA-approved sterile urologic irrigant - it is for irrigation only and must NEVER be given intravenously
Electrolyte-free / non-conductive so it does not disperse the electrosurgical current during TURP
Main danger is systemic absorption causing the TUR syndrome - dilutional hyponatremia, fluid overload, neurologic and visual disturbance
Limit irrigation pressure (reservoir height) and resection time, and watch instilled-versus-recovered volume to reduce absorption
Monitor serum sodium and mental/visual status; treat symptomatic hyponatremia carefully to avoid osmotic demyelination
Glycine metabolism can raise ammonia - consider hyperammonemia in postoperative confusion
missed: Not applicable - glycine irrigation is administered during a procedure by the surgical team and is not a self-administered scheduled medication.
overdose: Excessive absorption (effective overdose) produces the transurethral resection syndrome: acute dilutional hyponatremia, hypervolemia with pulmonary and cerebral edema, hypertension followed by hypotension and bradycardia, visual disturbance, confusion, seizures and coma. Management is to stop irrigation, restrict free water, support ventilation and circulation, give diuretics for fluid overload, and correct severe symptomatic hyponatremia carefully (e.g., hypertonic saline) at a controlled rate to avoid osmotic demyelination; treat hyperammonemia and seizures supportively.
